t: #3382 Maximum Area Rectangle With Point Constraints II
o: Find the largest axis-parallel rectangle whose four corners are given points and which contains no other point inside or on its border. In Example 2 the only corner-complete rectangle [1,1]–[3,3] traps (2,2), so the answer is -1. In Example 3 the tall rectangle is blocked by (1,2)/(3,2), leaving area 2. With n up to 2×10⁵, an O(n⁴) corner check is hopeless; we need a sweep over vertical columns.
k: Any valid rectangle's left and right edges are vertical pairs of points sharing the same x-coordinate.
Sweep columns left→right; for each pair of y-values in a column, remember the last x where that pair could anchor a left edge.
A pair becomes unusable forever once a column contains a point strictly between its two y-values, since every future rectangle spanning that column would contain it.
Grouping work per column bounds total pair work by O(n²) worst case, typically far less.

a.n: Approach 1: Column Sweep with Pair Memory
a.i: Process points grouped by x in increasing order. Within a column, consider every pair of y-values as a potential vertical edge. If this (y₁,y₂) pair was previously anchored at some earlier x′ with no blocking point in between, the rectangle spans area (x − x′)(y₂ − y₁). After checking, record the pair at the current x only if no point in this column lies strictly between y₁ and y₂; otherwise delete the pair, as it can never yield a clean rectangle again.
s: Sort points by x (ties by y); iterate over maximal groups of equal x.
For each pair (y_a, y_b) in the column, if stored with last x′, update the answer with (x − x′)(y_b − y_a).
Determine whether any point in this column has y strictly between y_a and y_b.
If unblocked, set last[(y_a,y_b)] = x; otherwise erase the entry.
a.t: O(n²) worst case — the sum of squared column sizes is bounded by n²; typically much faster on sparse columns.

a.n: Approach 2: Brute Force Quadruple Check (conceptual baseline)
a.i: Try every combination of two distinct x-values and two distinct y-values; if all four corners exist and no other point falls in the closed rectangle, record its area. This directly mirrors the definition and is useful for validating the sweep on small inputs.
s: Collect the sets of distinct x and y coordinates.
For each pair (x₁, x₂) and (y₁, y₂), verify all four corner points exist using a hash set.
Scan all points; reject the rectangle if any lies within [x₁,x₂]×[y₁,y₂].
Keep the maximum area over accepted rectangles.
a.t: O(X²Y² · n) in the worst case — far too slow for n = 2×10⁵, viable only for tiny inputs.

w: Always present the column sweep; the brute force is only a correctness reference. The subtlest part is the deletion rule: a pair blocked by an intermediate y in some column must be erased, not merely skipped, or you will emit rectangles containing that point. Watch out for points on the border (they block too — the closed-rectangle condition), duplicate handling (points are unique here), and coordinate compression if you extend to a BIT-based solution. Follow-ups: rectangles with sides not axis-parallel, or maximizing perimeter instead.
